shape.rule: A cost, stated plainly, aimed at the viewer, with the moral left out.
constraints: Second person or an object the viewer owns (phone, house, address book, Monday, midnight).
One concrete noun from ordinary life, not a virtue word.
A deadline or before/after: one last time, one year from tonight, before you, this year.
No advice. No 'so', 'remember', 'always', 'never forget', 'that is why'.
End on the consequence, not the lesson.

note: Drafts only. Nothing reads this file. To publish, append the lines to assets/quotes/bank.json with status "approved", bump the counts in tests/quote-bank.test.js, and run npm test.

lines.line: One year from tonight, this exact hour will either be the night you started or the night you almost did.
You can lose this year the same way you lost the last one: quietly, on a phone, telling yourself it starts Monday.
You will get one more Monday like this one, and you already know what you did with the last forty.
You will measure this year by what you did at six in the morning, not what you promised at midnight.
Your parents are getting older at the same speed you are getting comfortable.
There is a version of you that survives this year, and it is being built in the hours nobody sees.
You are not waiting for the right time. You are waiting to feel ready, and that is a different thing.
You did not come this far to be talked out of it by someone who has never tried.
You still check the last seen time of someone who stopped checking yours months ago.
You gave them the version of you that asked for nothing, and they took it as the price.
The photos are still there. The person who used to look at you like that is not.
You did not lose them all at once. You lost them in the small texts you decided not to send.
You keep the fight going in your head because it is the last room where they still answer.
One day their name will be a word you read instead of a pain you feel, and today is not that day.
You spent years asking to be chosen by people who were never in a position to choose you.
You learned to be low maintenance in a house that rewarded you for needing nothing.
You can trace the exact year you started shrinking yourself to fit rooms that never asked you to.
You call it being realistic, and it keeps feeling like giving up with better vocabulary.
You already know what to do. You are waiting for permission from someone who never had it either.
Your standards grew and your address book did not, and you keep calling that a coincidence.
